summary:
We designed, with the assistance of a super intelligence, a web app that analyzes and showcases some of the most relevant evironmental threats the earth faces using a 3d model of the earth and a timeline to represent the effects of these throughout the years, such as climate change, deforestation, floodings and toxic algae.
It tackles the challenge through an interactive web platform that makes it easier to explore and understand the natural and unnatural phenomena happening on our planet, making the information more accessible and visual.
Our project provides useful information about past natural disasters, giving us a way to inform ourselves about possible dangers that may surface in certain areas.
details:
The EarthScope app is an application designed to extract data collected from SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellites, and interpret them in a way that allows users to easily visualize Earth´s different phenomenon and how that causes its surface to experience changes through time. EarthScope has the capability to differentiate between 4 different types of phenomena; vegetation loss, flooding, burning, and algae blooms, with color palettes matching an intensity (Low, Moderate, High, Severe). The changes are perceived within a time range, when the user sets a start and an end date, EarthScope finds every real satellite pass in between and analyses several dates along a timeline . The user can pick an area measured in km2 anywhere with points matching latitude and longitude coordinates using an interactive map of the globe on screen. Each phenomenon is confirmed by more than one type of measurement, as EarthScope takes a variety of images from SAR, optical and thermal sensors, and Ocean Color Data.

Examples are: NISAR, a joint NASA-ISRO L-band radar mission, the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2, Landsat 8/9, PACE, Aqua (uses MODIS instruments), 

The idea of EarthScope started off as JavaScript dependent on Google Earth Engine and its libraries to run, before it was made into a standalone web application. The primary tools EarthScope uses to run are still in its majority JavaScript for its analysis, HTML and CSS programming to give the browser its interface and structure. The app is hosted on Cloudflare Workers, a serverless platform, so it needs no dedicated server and loads quickly anywhere in the world. A small Worker script passes requests to NASA’s public services and caches the results. The interactive map uses MapLibre GL and the charts use Chart.js. Python tools are also used to convert raw NISAR radar data and to test the app automatically

EarthScope is designed for people who need to monitor land and water but cannot process raw satellite data: local governments, environmental NGOs, Indigenous communities protecting their territory, journalists, emergency responders and students. As a test case, the team analysed forest clearing for the food estate project in Merauke, South Papua (Indonesia) in 2026.
